title: Ticket Booking System: Complete Architecture
description: Design a concert and event ticket booking platform (Ticketmaster / BookMyShow) with virtual waiting rooms, distributed seat locking, and flash-sale concurrency control.

data.text: Design an event and concert ticketing platform like Ticketmaster or BookMyShow. The system hosts stadium-scale concerts (80,000 seats) and movie theaters. During high-demand flash sales (e.g. Taylor Swift Eras Tour), 5+ million concurrent fans attempt to reserve the same finite pool of seats within seconds. The central engineering challenge is extreme write contention: the system must prevent overselling with 100% strict consistency, maintain an interactive real-time seat map, enforce a temporary 10-minute seat hold while users enter payment details, and protect core databases using a Virtual Waiting Room queue.

terms.definition: A front-door admission queue that throttles incoming traffic, issuing signed JWT queue tokens to let users enter seat selection at a controlled rate (e.g. 1,000 users/sec).
An atomic lock placed on specific seat IDs in an in-memory Redis cluster with a 10-minute TTL, reserving them while the customer checks out.
Phase 1: Reserve seat in Redis (Soft Hold). Phase 2: Authorize payment and write immutable booking record to PostgreSQL (Hard Commit).
Representing stadium seat availability as compressed bit arrays in memory for ultra-fast rendering on user browsers.
A background scheduler monitoring expired Redis seat holds to release abandoned seats back into the available pool.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Event Discovery: Search and browse events by artist, venue, city, date, and price category
Interactive Seat Map: Display real-time visual seat availability (Available, Held, Booked)
Seat Hold (10-Minute Lock): Allow users to hold up to 6 seats for 10 minutes while completing checkout
Checkout & Payment: Process payment securely and atomically transition seats from Held to Confirmed
Automatic Hold Expiration: Release held seats immediately if the 10-minute timer lapses or payment fails
E-Ticket Delivery: Generate cryptographically signed digital tickets with dynamic fraud-resistant QR codes

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Zero Double-Booking: Absolute 100% guarantee that no single seat is ever sold to more than one customer
Flash-Sale Concurrency: Absorb 100,000+ seat reservation attempts per second during peak drops
Seat Map Latency: <100ms P99 latency for seat map status queries
Hold Precision: Seat hold timers must expire accurately within 1 second of the 10-minute mark
Availability: 99.999% uptime for the front-door queue; 99.99% for payment checkout

data.text: To protect backend databases from being crushed by millions of simultaneous requests, the architecture places a Virtual Waiting Room at the edge. Only admitted users with valid cryptographically signed tokens can access the Seat Selection and Checkout services.

data.caption: Ticket Booking Architecture: Virtual Waiting Room, Edge CDN, In-Memory Seat Lock Engine (Redis), SAGA Checkout, and Ticket Generator

data.text: The booking sequence enforces an atomic soft-hold in Redis. Only if the seat lock succeeds does the user advance to payment. A payment timeout or card decline automatically releases the lock.

data.caption: Seat reservation sequence: Redis atomic Lua hold, checkout payment authorization, and permanent DB commit

faqs.question: Why is a Virtual Waiting Room mandatory for concert flash sales?
faqs.answer: Without a waiting room, 5 million users clicking "Refresh" at 10:00:00 AM hits origin servers with tens of gigabits of un-cacheable write traffic, crashing API gateways and connection pools. The waiting room acts as a traffic dam at the edge (Cloudflare/AWS CloudFront), queuing requests and admitting only 1,000 users per second — exactly matching the downstream processing capacity.

faqs.question: How does an atomic Redis Lua script prevent race conditions during seat holds?
faqs.answer: Redis executes Lua scripts atomically in a single-threaded event loop. The script verifies that none of the requested seat keys exist: `for i, seat in ipairs(KEYS) do if redis.call("exists", seat) == 1 then return 0 end end`. If all are free, it sets all keys with a 600-second TTL. Because no other command can interleave, two concurrent requests for the same seat can never both succeed.

faqs.question: What happens if a user closes the browser or their phone dies during a 10-minute hold?
faqs.answer: The held seats in Redis have a strict 600-second TTL. When the key expires, Redis emits an expiration event via Keyspace Notifications (or an Expiration Daemon scans expired leases). A worker releases the seats back to available status on the live seat map, allowing waitlisted fans to select them.

faqs.question: How do you prevent fraudulent ticket scalping and barcode duplication?
faqs.answer: Ticketmaster uses rotating dynamic barcodes (SafeTix). The client application displays a QR code generated from a rolling cryptographic TOTP (Time-Based One-Time Password) that refreshes every 15 seconds. Screenshots and printouts cannot be scanned at venue turnstiles.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Virtual Waiting Rooms at the edge throttle millions of fans into a controlled downstream flow
Redis atomic Lua scripts lock multiple seat keys simultaneously with zero race conditions
Two-phase reservation: fast in-memory soft hold (10-minute TTL) precedes durable SQL hard commit
TTL expiration daemons ensure abandoned seats return to the available inventory pool automatically
Dynamic rotating QR codes (TOTP) protect digital tickets from unauthorized duplication and scalping
data.takeaway: Ticket booking systems survive extreme flash-sale spikes by shielding transactional databases behind edge waiting rooms and utilizing atomic in-memory Redis locks to enforce absolute zero double-booking.
